tagline: An old highway alternate through eroded buttes and mixed-grass prairie
intro: South Dakota Highway 240, signed as the Badlands Loop, crosses the eastern portion of Badlands National Park. The park protects sharply eroded buttes and pinnacles alongside mixed-grass prairie. Exposed rock records a change from inland sea to river floodplains; erosion continues to shape the badlands. The Yellow Mounds expose an old soil that weathered on marine rocks. Above that soil, the White River Group records river and floodplain deposits; volcanic ash from eruptions in the present-day Great Basin survives in the upper beds.

A highway was part of the park’s beginnings: the 1929 law authorizing Badlands National Monument made construction of a 30-mile road through it a condition of its eventual proclamation. Construction on the highway began in the early 1930s, and the loop had a gravel surface by 1944. By the late 1940s, it carried the US 16 Alternate number. When US 16 was cut back to Rapid City around 1980, its alternate no longer met the parent route and became SD 240.
From Wall at Interstate 90’s exit 110, the road runs south into the park and turns southeast. At park headquarters at Cedar Pass, it turns northeast to rejoin I-90 at exit 131 near Cactus Flat.
notice: The park’s exposed rock records the shift from an inland sea to river floodplains.

moments.title: Wall
moments.text: Wall began as a railroad town, platted in 1907 when the Chicago and North Western reached this point. Its name comes from the natural wall of rock formations by the Badlands. A different kind of traffic helped make it known later: Ted Hustead bought Wall Drug in 1931, and Dorothy Hustead proposed advertising free ice water to travelers heading toward Mount Rushmore. The original pharmacy stood on Route 16A, the highway number once carried by the loop. The small pharmacy grew into a roadside attraction. Wall also houses the National Grasslands Visitor Center, a companion subject to the park’s rock formations.

moments.title: Interior
moments.text: Interior moved to meet the railroad. Its earlier life began as a freighting way-station established by George and Louis Johnson on the White River in 1883. In 1907 and 1908, the settlement shifted two and a half miles northwest along the river to the Milwaukee Railroad; the previous site became old Interior. A water system followed in 1910 and an electric grid in 1912. In 1919, 1921 and 1922, roundups brought tourists by train from as far away as Minneapolis. Interior lies along the White River approximately one mile from Badlands National Park.

moments.title: Ben Reifel Visitor Center
moments.text: The Ben Reifel Visitor Center dates from 1957–58, when it was built under the Mission 66 plan for Badlands National Monument. The monument became a national park in 1978. The monument was established to preserve natural scenery and educational resources, with scientific excavation specifically authorized. The center offers museum exhibits, special programs and a bookstore. Nearby, the park’s established trails include Cliff Shelf Nature Trail. The landscape outside has a much longer record: the exposed rocks document an inland sea giving way to river floodplains, and erosion has cut the rocks into walls, buttes and pinnacles.

practical: Wall: A national park entrance fee is charged where the highway enters the park. (checked 2026-10-11)
